summary: An overview for new Internet users, answering commonly asked questions in a consumer-friendly way. It is informational and replaced RFC 1594.

eli5.summary: A beginner's question and answer page about the Internet, written for ordinary people.

subtitle: A plain-language Q and A that explains the Internet to ordinary new users in 1999.

tldr.problem: New, non-technical Internet users kept asking the same basic questions, and earlier guides were aimed at more technical readers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo answers them in plain language: what the Internet is, what you can do on it, what addresses mean, how it works, who runs it and how to stay safe.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1594 as FYI 4 and points readers who want more depth to FYI 7.

today: RFC 2664 is an Informational memo (FYI 4) that obsoletes RFC 1594, and no RFC is listed as replacing it. It is a 1999 snapshot written for consumers of that era.

sections.title: Who This Guide Is For
sections.content:
This memo is an overview for the new Internet user. It takes a consumer-oriented approach and avoids depth. Unlike its predecessors, it answers the general questions an unsophisticated consumer would ask rather than the pointed questions of a technical user, and it sends readers who want intermediate and advanced topics to FYI 7.

It begins with the basics: computers connected together form a network, and networks joined by specialized computers called routers make up the Internet. Home users typically connect over a telephone line using a modem.
sections.eli5: The Internet is lots of computer groups hooked together so people can share things. This guide explains it simply.

sections.title: What You Can Do Online
sections.content:
The memo lists the main activities: surfing, searching, e-mail, file transfer, chat, games, and shopping, banking and investing. Surfing uses a web browser to follow links from one information site to another, like footnotes in a printed work. Searching uses a search engine, compared to a library card catalog, and different engines give different lists.

E-mail is likened to post office letters or office memos, and readers are pointed to the Netiquette Guidelines (RFC 1855). Mailing lists are a major source of junk e-mail, so users should not be the source of spam. Files move by e-mail attachment, a browser's save feature or FTP. Chat is compared to a party, where some people only listen and some may pretend to be someone else.

For shopping and banking, the memo cautions users to check that security features protect their credit card information, and to avoid a site that will not say how it protects them.
sections.eli5: You can read pages, look things up, send letters, trade files, chat and play games. Just be careful who you talk to and where you type your card number.

sections.title: E-mail Addresses and URLs
sections.content:
People often ask for an e-mail address (where to send information) or a URL (where to get it). An e-mail address such as myname@company.com has two parts split by an @ sign. The left part is like the name line on a letter and is assigned by the system administrator. The right part names the computer system providing the mail service, usually a company name plus a domain such as edu, com or a country code like fr or jp. The right part is what is used to find the destination computer.

A URL such as http://www.newspaper.com also has two parts, divided by //. The left part says which kind of service to look for, and the right part names the computer providing it. A longer form such as http://www.newspaper.com/sports/article1.html points to a specific article.
sections.eli5: An e-mail address is like a name and a street on an envelope. A URL tells your browser which computer to visit and which page to open.

sections.title: How the Internet Works and Who Runs It
sections.content:
Computers take turns being the source and the destination. Each has a unique Internet address, and routers at interconnection points use that address to point information on its way. The memo gives a simplified conversation: the source finds the destination's address, they exchange hellos, the source breaks its data into small packets, routers guide each packet, the destination reassembles them and confirms receipt, and both sides say good bye. It admits this skips details such as address discovery and how packets are split and rebuilt.

On who runs the Internet, the answer is no one. It is a cooperative effort among Internet Service Providers, software companies, volunteer organizations and a few facilities that tie it together. ISPs agree to connect to each other following protocols, some organizations assign addresses much as telephone numbers are assigned, others track names, and the volunteer Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) develops the protocols.

The memo also gives etiquette tips: there is no single formal rulebook, e-mail lacks tone of voice so people use capitals and emoticons such as :-), and a document sent as an attachment may be unreadable unless the receiver has the same program, so a plain text version is safer.
sections.eli5: Your computer chops a message into little pieces, routers pass the pieces along like mail sorters, and the other computer puts them back together. Nobody owns the whole thing.

sections.title: Staying Safe
sections.content:
The memo says that "is the Internet secure?" is confusing because people hear both assurances and scary stories, and offers three rules of thumb.

  • Never share account passwords. Learning a password is the easiest way to break into a system. See the Users' Security Handbook (RFC 2504).
  • Understand that email, downloads and sites visited can be tracked. Administrators need access to such information, and old e-mail or browsing logs may survive on backup tapes.
  • Before giving personal information in a web form, realize there is no assurance of confidentiality or privacy. It is compared to faxing the information to a party you have never dealt with.
sections.eli5: Keep your password secret, remember that what you do online may be recorded, and think before you type personal details into a website.

references.text: Guttman, E., Leong, G. and G. Malkin, "Users' Security Handbook", FYI 34, RFC 2504, February 1999.
